Wellness and distress as two continua

Source: R/igm.R
dualcont.Rd

For each group, one wellness indicator against one distress indicator, each with its published interval, and the ratio of the two: the dual-continua view of mental health, in which wellness is not the absence of distress and is measured in its own right.

Usage

dualcont(x, well, distress, conflvl = 0.95)

Arguments

x

A wellness profile from welprof.

well, distress

One wellness and one distress indicator of x.

conflvl

Confidence level of the published intervals and of the ratio (default 0.95).

Value

A data frame of class dualcont with group, wellness, wello, welup, distress, distrlo, distrup, strratio, ratiolo, ratioup and usewithcau.

Details

Keyes (2002, 2005) showed that flourishing and mental illness are correlated but distinct axes: a person, or a population, can carry distress and also wellness. That is how Indigenous scholars of mental health describe it too, as wellness and as a process of healing rather than as illness alone (Stewart 2008). Plotting the groups on both axes keeps a strength visible beside the burden it sits next to. The strratio is \(R = W / D\), wellness over distress, with the log-normal interval \(\exp\{\log R \pm z\sqrt{\sigma_W^2 + \sigma_D^2}\}\) from the two published intervals: above 1, more people report the wellness than the distress. The two estimates come from the same respondents; their covariance is not published, so the interval treats them as independent and is too narrow when they are negatively correlated, as answers about wellness and distress usually are. Any two indicators on one scale can be set against each other.

Acknowledgement

This estimator puts to quantitative use the framework of Professor Suzanne Stewart (Yellowknives Dene First Nation, University of Toronto).

See the acknowledgements in the section on Indigenous health of the package's vignette (vignette("crimlab")).

References

Keyes CLM (2002). The mental health continuum: from languishing to flourishing in life. Journal of Health and Social Behavior 43(2):207-222. doi:10.2307/3090197

Keyes CLM (2005). Mental illness and/or mental health? Investigating axioms of the complete state model of health. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 73(3):539-548. doi:10.1037/0022-006X.73.3.539

Stewart SL (2008), see holbal.

See also

welprof.

Examples

# your own table: made-up percentages for two communities, with limits
own <- data.frame(
  community = rep(c("Lakeside", "Riverbend"), each = 4),
  item = rep(c("Hopeful", "Satisfied", "Rarely hopeful", "Low satisfaction"),
             2),
  pct = c(64, 71, 12, 18, 58, 66, 16, 22),
  lo = c(59, 66, 9, 14, 52, 60, 12, 17),
  hi = c(69, 76, 15, 22, 64, 72, 20, 27)
)
w <- welprof(own, "community", "item", "pct", "lo", "hi",
             well = "Hopeful", distress = "Rarely hopeful")
dualcont(w, "Hopeful", "Rarely hopeful")
#> Dual continuum: wellness beside distress
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Wellness: Hopeful
#> Distress: Rarely hopeful
#> Groups:   2
#> Ratio:    wellness over distress, log-normal interval
#> 
#>     group  wellness  interval  distress  interval   ratio  ratio interval
#>  Lakeside        64  [59, 69]        12    [9, 15]  5.333    [4.08, 6.97]
#> Riverbend        58  [52, 64]        16   [12, 20]  3.625    [2.75, 4.78]
#> 
#> A ratio above 1: more people report the wellness than the distress.
#> 2 of 2 groups have the whole interval above 1.
#> 
#> Both estimates come from the same respondents and their covariance
#> is not published: the interval treats them as independent.
